entry: Triple star system in the southern constellation of [[Centaurus]]. Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri A) and Toliman (Alpha Centauri B) are Sun-like stars, of classes G and K, that form the [[Binary star|binary]] system α Centauri AB, which orbits a common center with an orbital period of 79 years. Their elliptical orbit varies the distance between them from 35.6 astronomical units (AU) to 11.2 AU. Proxima Centauri (Alpha Centauri C) is a small, faint [[Red dwarf|red dwarf]] and the closest star to the Sun, at 4.2465 light-years (1.3020 parsecs). It has two confirmed planets, Proxima b and Proxima d. Seen with the naked eye, Alpha Centauri AB appears as a single star with an apparent magnitude of −0.27; it is the brightest star in the constellation and the third-brightest in the night sky.

Ionizing particle of two protons and two neutrons, identical to the nucleus of a helium-4 atom. Alpha particles, also called alpha rays or alpha radiation, are named after the Greek letter α. They are generally produced in [[Radioactive decay|alpha decay]] but may also arise in other ways. The term was coined by [[Ernest Rutherford]] while he studied uranium radiation. Standard alpha decay produces alpha particles with a kinetic energy of about 5 MeV and a velocity of about 4% of the speed of light. They are highly [[Ionization|ionizing]] but penetrate little, stopped by a few centimeters of air or by the skin. Helium nuclei, which form 10–12% of cosmic rays, are usually of much higher energy and can penetrate far more deeply. Once an alpha particle gains electrons, it becomes a neutral helium atom.

American technology conglomerate holding company, headquartered in Mountain View, California. Created through a restructuring of [[Google]] on October 2, 2015, it became the parent of Google and several former Google subsidiaries. It is listed on the Nasdaq under the tickers GOOGL and GOOG. Founders [[Larry Page]] and [[Sergey Brin]] stepped down from executive posts in December 2019 but remain controlling shareholders. In 2023 the company faced widespread criticism for mass layoffs affecting 12,000 employees. It has faced antitrust actions in the United States, France and Japan.

Pastime and sport of sliding down snow-covered slopes on skis with fixed-heel bindings. Unlike [[Skiing|other forms of skiing]] such as cross-country, Telemark and [[Ski jumping|ski jumping]], which use free-heel bindings, alpine skiing is typically practiced at ski resorts with lifts and artificial snowmaking. Off-piste skiers may be carried to the top of slopes by snowmobile or helicopter. Alpine ski racing has been held at the Winter Olympics since 1936, and the FIS World Cup circuit began in 1966. Racing events include downhill, slalom, giant slalom, super-G and alpine combined. The sport is governed by the Fédération Internationale de Ski et de Snowboard (FIS).

Major mountain range of Central Europe, about 1,200 km (750 mi) long. It stretches across Monaco, [[France]], [[Switzerland]], [[Italy]], Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. The range formed over tens of millions of years as the African and Eurasian tectonic plates collided, thrusting marine sedimentary rock into peaks such as [[Mont Blanc]] and the [[Matterhorn]]. It contains 82 peaks higher than 4,000 m (13,000 ft). Evidence of human habitation dates to the Paleolithic era. [[Hannibal]] crossed the Alps with elephants, and in 1800 [[Napoleon]] crossed one of its passes with an army of 40,000. Tourism became the dominant industry by the end of the 20th century. As of 2010 the region had 14 million residents and 120 million annual visitors. The [[Winter Olympic Games]] have been held in its Swiss, French, Italian, Austrian and German parts.

Cultural region and territorial collectivity of northeastern [[France]] (pop., 2021: 1,919,745), on the west bank of the upper Rhine. Its largest city is [[Strasbourg]]. Alsace was part of the [[Holy Roman Empire]], was annexed by France after the [[Thirty Years' War]], and was part of the [[German Empire]] from 1871. It returned to France in 1919 and, after reincorporation into Germany in 1940, became French again after 1944. Since 2016 it has been part of the Grand Est region, though in April 2026 the French National Assembly approved a bill to separate Alsace from it; the bill had yet to pass the Senate.

Genus of about 128 South American flowering plants in the family Alstroemeriaceae, commonly called Peruvian lilies or lilies of the Incas. Most species are restricted to one of two centers of diversity: central [[Chile]] and southern [[Argentina]], or eastern [[Brazil]]. Patagonian species grow in winter, while Brazilian species grow in summer. The plants grow from clusters of tubers, and each flower has six petals up to 5 centimeters long. Many hybrids and at least 190 cultivars have been developed, and cut flowers survive up to 14 days in water. The genus is named after the Swedish baron Clas Alströmer, a friend of [[Carl Linnaeus]].

Mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, [[Mongolia]] and Kazakhstan converge. The rivers Irtysh and [[Ob]] rise in the range, whose highest summit is Belukha, at 4,506 m (14,783 ft) above sea level. The massif merges with the Sayan Mountains to the northeast and into the [[Gobi Desert]] plateau to the southeast; the [[Tian Shan]] lies beyond the Junggar Basin to the southwest. The sparse, ethnically diverse population includes [[Turkic peoples]] and [[Mongols]]. The local economy is based on livestock husbandry, hunting, agriculture, forestry and mining. The range is a [[World Heritage Site]] in its Russian part, and the now discredited Altaic language family takes its name from it.

Brightest star in the constellation Aquila, and the twelfth-brightest in the night sky. It has an apparent visual magnitude of 0.77 and lies 16.7 light-years (5.1 parsecs) from the Sun. Altair is an A-type [[Main sequence|main-sequence]] star of about 1.8 times the Sun's mass, and one of the vertices of the Summer Triangle, with [[Vega]] and Deneb. It rotates rapidly, at about 286 km/s at its equator, and is flattened at the poles. It is classed as a Delta Scuti variable star.

Table or platform on which religious offerings, sacrifices or other ritual acts are made. Altars are found at shrines, temples, churches and other places of worship. They are used particularly in [[Christianity]], Buddhism, Hinduism and modern paganism, and were used in the Roman, Greek and Norse religions. In ancient Roman religion, altars were often inscribed with the donor's name and the deity honored; the Ara Pacis was dedicated by [[Augustus]] to the goddess Pax. The first altar recorded in the Hebrew Bible was erected by [[Noah]] after the flood. In Catholic and Orthodox theology the table on which the [[Eucharist]] is consecrated is an altar, since the Eucharist re-presents the sacrifice of Christ. Churches generally have a single altar, often on higher ground and set apart from the rest of the church.

Electric current alternating in direction, unlike [[Direct current|direct current]] (DC). It is the form in which electric power is delivered to homes and businesses, and its usual waveform is a sine wave. Power is transmitted at high voltage because the power lost in a wire equals the square of the current multiplied by the wire's resistance (P = I²R); halving the current by doubling the voltage cuts the loss by a factor of four. [[Transformer|Transformers]] step voltage up for transmission and down for use, typically to 100 V–240 V for domestic supply. Alternating current prevailed over direct current in the late 19th century; Niagara Falls was electrified with AC transmission lines in 1895.

Life cycle of plants and algae in which haploid and diploid multicellular phases alternate. A mature [[Sporophyte|sporophyte]] produces haploid spores by [[Meiosis|meiosis]]; the spores grow into haploid [[Gametophyte|gametophytes]], which produce gametes by [[Mitosis|mitosis]]. Two gametes fuse to form a diploid zygote that develops into a new sporophyte. In liverworts, mosses and hornworts the gametophyte is dominant and the sporophyte depends on it. In ferns the gametophyte is a small prothallus, and in [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] it consists of just a few cells growing inside the sporophyte. Animals produce gametes directly and generally have no multicellular haploid phase.

Range of processes in which a third party helps disputing parties settle a dispute short of [[Lawsuit|litigation]]. Also called external dispute resolution, it is increasingly used within court systems as well as outside them. The term arose from Frank Sander’s paper “Varieties of Dispute Processing.” In 2008 some courts required parties to try mediation before trial; the European Mediation Directive contemplates compulsory mediation, meaning attendance is required but settlement is not. In England and Wales it is often called NCDR (Non Court Dispute Resolution). Supporters cite rising court caseloads, lower costs than litigation, confidentiality and control over who decides. Critics of mandatory arbitration in employment and consumer contracts argue that it may curtail discovery, appeals and transparency.

Healing practices outside mainstream evidence-based medicine, which aim to produce the effects of medicine without supporting evidence of effectiveness. Unlike modern medicine, these therapies are generally not tested by the [[Scientific method|scientific method]] of clinical trials, and may rely on testimonials, tradition or belief in supernatural energies. Some are based on theories that contradict established science of how the body works. Much of the perceived effect is attributed to the [[Placebo|placebo]] effect or to the natural course of disease. Some therapies are actively harmful, such as cyanide poisoning from amygdalin or the intentional ingestion of [[Hydrogen peroxide|hydrogen peroxide]]. Traditional medicine becomes “alternative” when used outside its original setting without scientific explanation. Billions of dollars have been spent studying alternative medicine, with few or no positive results.

Category of rock music rooted in the independent underground of the 1970s. The term “alternative” refers to the genre’s distinction from mainstream or commercial rock and pop; its original meaning was broader, referring to musicians influenced by late-1970s punk rock and its DIY ethos. In September 1988 *Billboard* introduced “alternative” into its charting system to reflect the format’s growth on United States radio. The genre reached the mainstream in the 1990s with the grunge movement in the United States and with Britpop and [[Shoegaze|shoegaze]] in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Nirvana’s 1991 album *Nevermind* was a breakthrough. In the 2000s, emo-influenced acts such as [[Fall Out Boy]], [[My Chemical Romance]] and [[Paramore]] achieved multi-platinum success.

Plateau in west-central South America, the most extensive high plateau on Earth outside Tibet. The name is Spanish for “high plain.” It lies mostly in [[Bolivia]], with northern parts in Peru, southwestern fringes in [[Chile]] and extensions into [[Argentina]]. Its average elevation is approximately 3,650 meters (12,000 feet). [[Lake Titicaca]], South America’s largest lake, lies on the Bolivia–Peru border at 3,810 meters. Lake Poopó, formerly Bolivia’s second-largest lake, had completely dried up by December 2015. The plateau was home to the Chiripa, Tiwanaku and [[Inca Empire|Inca]] cultures before Spain conquered the region in the 16th century. Mining, llama and vicuña herding, and urban services are the major economic activities today.

Concern for the well-being and life of others, independent of personal benefit or reciprocity. The word was popularized, and possibly coined, by French philosopher [[Auguste Comte]] around 1830 as an antonym of egoism. Altruism is an important moral value in many cultures and religions, and it can extend to other sentient beings and future generations. In biology, altruism is an action that costs the actor, in time, energy or survival probability, while benefiting another without reciprocity. Psychological egoism holds that no act is truly altruistic, since the actor may gain an intrinsic reward; whether such rewards count as benefits is disputed. Effective altruism uses evidence and reason to determine the most effective ways to benefit others.

Family of hydrated double sulfate salts of [[Aluminium|aluminum]], with the general formula XAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, where X is a monovalent cation such as potassium or ammonium. Potassium alum, KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O, is the best known; sodium and ammonium alums are named for their cations. The name also covers analogues in which aluminum is replaced by another trivalent metal, most commonly [[Chromium|chromium]], as in chrome alum, KCr(SO₄)₂·12H₂O. In industry “alum” usually means aluminum sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃·nH₂O, used as a flocculant in water treatment and papermaking. In medicine the term can refer to aluminum hydroxide gel, used as a vaccine adjuvant.

Chemical element (symbol Al, atomic number 13), a post-transition metal in the [[Boron|boron]] group. Silvery, soft, ductile and nonmagnetic, aluminum has a density about one-third that of steel. It forms a protective oxide layer when exposed to air. It is the third-most abundant element in Earth’s crust, after [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and [[Silicon|silicon]], occurring mainly in rock rather than as free metal, and is obtained industrially from [[Bauxite|bauxite]]. Its discovery was announced in 1825 by [[Hans Christian Ørsted]]. Mass production became possible after the Hall–Héroult process, developed independently in 1886 by Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France. In 1954 aluminum became the most produced non-ferrous metal, surpassing [[Copper|copper]]. Most is used in transportation, engineering, construction and packaging. No living thing is known to metabolize aluminum salts, though plants and animals tolerate them well.

Chemical compound of aluminum and oxygen, Al₂O₃, commonly called alumina. It is refined from [[Bauxite|bauxite]] and is the feedstock for aluminum metal. Naturally it occurs as the mineral [[Corundum|corundum]], whose varieties form the gemstones [[Ruby|ruby]] and [[Sapphire|sapphire]]. Its hardness makes it useful as an abrasive, and its high melting point of 2,072 °C makes it a refractory material.

Finnish architect and designer. His work includes buildings, furniture, textiles and glassware, as well as sculptures and paintings, though he did not regard himself as an artist. His early work drew on Nordic Classicism, his 1930s work on a rational International Style [[Modernism|modernism]], and his work from the 1940s on a more organic style. He designed buildings together with their interiors, furniture and lamps as a *Gesamtkunstwerk*, or total work of art, often with his first wife, architect Aino Aalto. His bent plywood furniture influenced Charles and Ray Eames and George Nelson. Notable works include the Paimio Tuberculosis Sanatorium, the Viipuri Library, Villa Mairea and Finlandia Hall in [[Helsinki]]. His work was shaped by European modernists associated with the [[Bauhaus]].

Clade of protists, considered a major group within the Eukaryota. Alveolates are unified by cortical alveoli, flattened membrane-bound sacs beneath the plasma membrane. Their three main lineages are the [[Dinoflagellate|dinoflagellates]], which can form harmful algal blooms; the [[Apicomplexa|apicomplexans]], obligate intracellular parasites that cause malaria and toxoplasmosis; and the [[Ciliate|ciliates]], covered in hair-like cilia used for locomotion and feeding, which include the model organism [[Paramecium]]. Alveolates are grouped with the [[Stramenopile|stramenopiles]] and [[Rhizaria]] in the SAR supergroup, and a 2015 classification ranks the group as a superphylum.

Progressive neurodegenerative disease and the most common cause of [[Dementia|dementia]], accounting for around 60–70% of cases. It usually begins with difficulty remembering recent events. As it advances it can cause problems with language, disorientation, mood swings and withdrawal from family and society. Its progression is characterized by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]], which lead to irreversible loss of [[Neuron|neurons]]. The strongest genetic risk factor is an allele of apolipoprotein E. No known treatment can stop or reverse progression, though some may temporarily improve symptoms. The disease is named after German psychiatrist and pathologist Alois Alzheimer, who first described it in 1906. As of 2020 about 50 million people worldwide had the disease.

2001 French romantic comedy film directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet. Written by Jeunet with Guillaume Laurant, *Amélie* follows a shy waitress, played by Audrey Tautou, who decides to change the lives of those around her while dealing with her own isolation in Montmartre, Paris. Released in France on April 25, 2001, it won four César Awards, including Best Film and Best Director, and was nominated for five [[Academy Awards]]. It grossed $174.2 million worldwide against a budget of $10 million.

Alloy of [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] with one or more other metals, existing as a liquid, soft paste or solid depending on its proportions. Amalgams form through metallic bonding. Many metals form amalgams with mercury, but iron, platinum, tungsten and tantalum are notable exceptions. Gold–mercury amalgam is used to extract [[Gold|gold]] from [[Ore|ore]], and dental amalgams are made with metals such as silver, copper, indium, tin and [[Zinc|zinc]]. Zinc amalgam serves as a reducing agent in the Clemmensen reduction. Dental amalgam releases trace mercury vapor, particularly when chewed; regulatory assessments affirm general safety while acknowledging risks for sensitive populations.
